items.abstract: <jats:p>Automated Linux driver generation requires machine-readable representations that capture hardware resources, device behavior, Linux kernel contracts, and validation evidence. Although many such representations have emerged across hardware-description standards, driver synthesis systems, Linux engineering frameworks, and verification tools, their roles in supporting driver generation remain fragmented and insufficiently understood. This paper presents a problemoriented thematic survey of hardware-driver intermediate representations (IRs) for peripheraldriver generation, covering 75 papers, standards, and engineering documents from 1997 to May 2026. We organize existing techniques with a two-dimensional taxonomy of semantic content and usage form, and compare representative mechanisms including Device Tree, ACPI, IP-XACT, SystemRDL, CMSIS-SVD, regmap, driver DSLs, Termite, Dingo/Tingu, Coccinelle, syzlang, eBPF/HID-BPF, Pancake/Viper/Sockeye, and structured representations for large-languagemodel-based generation. The survey shows that static hardware facts and platform configuration have relatively mature representations, while behavioral protocols, DMA ownership, security boundaries, cross-kernel-version adaptation, and reproducible evaluation remain insufficiently supported. Based on these findings, we outline a research agenda centered on hardware-driver alignment IR (HDA-IR) and public benchmarks for trustworthy, verifiable, and reproducible Linux peripheral-driver generation.</jats:p>
title: A Survey of Intermediate Representations for Linux Driver Generation: Toward Bridging Hardware Facts, Behavioral Contracts, Linux Contracts, and Validation Feedback

items.abstract: <jats:p>The increasing use of Large Language Models (LLMs) on consumer devices raises practical concerns regarding inference latency and resource efficiency, which can vary depending on the operating system environment. However, it is still unknown which operating system is most optimal and efficient for executing local LLM workloads on hardware with limited resources. Therefore, this study aims to compare and evaluate the inference performance of LLMs across three operating system environments: native Windows, Windows Subsystem for Linux 2 (WSL2), and native Linux on a low-spec laptop equipped with a 12th Gen Intel Core i3 processor and 8 GB of RAM. The Ollama framework is used to run several lightweight LLM models, including Llama3.2:3B, Qwen2.5:3B, and Phi3.5:3.8B. An experimental benchmarking approach is conducted using three levels of prompt complexity (light, medium, and heavy), with 10 trials for each prompt scenario to ensure consistency of results. Evaluation metrics include inference latency, CPU utilization, and memory consumption during model execution. Results show that the operating system environment significantly impacts the inference performance of LLMs. For example, using the Llama3.2:3B model under heavy prompting, the average latency reaches 71.24 seconds on Windows, 75.96 seconds on WSL2, and 70.80 seconds on native Linux, while under light prompting the average latency is 11.76 seconds, 12.73 seconds, and 10.83 seconds, respectively. These findings indicate that native Linux generally provides more efficient LLM inference on resource-constrained hardware. This study contributes an empirical and repeatable comparison across operating system environments, providing practical insights for selecting deployment platforms for LLM applications.</jats:p>
title: LLM INFERENCE PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS ACROSS WINDOWS, WINDOWS SUBSYSTEM FOR LINUX 2 AND NATIVE LINUX

items.abstract: <jats:p>Linux has long been celebrated for its stability, versatility, and open-source community support. However, even robust Unix-like systems face threats ranging from opportunistic malware to sophisticated nation-state attacks. Traditional server hardening practices file permission lockdowns, process whitelisting, configuration auditing still matters but can be overwhelmed by the complexity of large-scale or fast-changing infrastructures. This paper explores how AI techniques complement established security measures, from anomaly detection in logs to intelligent process monitoring. By marrying core Unix security principles with machine learning (ML)-based analytics, organizations can safeguard mission-critical servers from zero-day exploits, stealthy intrusions, and misconfigurations. We discuss real-world use cases, highlight key tools, and share recommended workflows to deploy AIdriven threat prevention on Linux systems.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Linux kernel specialization can improve system efficiency, but configuration changes may also alter functionality, compatibility, and security. Performance gains are difficult to interpret unless the configuration that was realized and executed is established. Existing configuration-tailoring, performance-search, and LLM-assisted methods address parts of this problem separately. They do not connect workload-derived evidence, model proposals, deterministic Kconfig realization, booted-state identity, empirical performance, and deployment-policy compliance in one auditable process. Intelligent Kernel Configuration (IKC) addresses this gap through an evidence-bounded workflow. Workload traces guide candidate selection, and local Kconfig knowledge constrains LLM-assisted editing. Deterministic configuration tools establish realizable states, while boot-time configurations define experimental identity. Repeated measurements provide performance evidence, and an explicit policy gate determines deployment eligibility. Across representative web-serving, database, storage, media-processing, and scheduler workloads, IKC produced workload-dependent improvements over conventional configurations. Several workload classes retained supported advantages over machine-tailored alternatives. Evidence for the contribution of trace conditioning was more concentrated, and explicit hardening constraints preserved much of the measured performance. Complementary network-path and performance-oriented comparisons were consistent with this interpretation. These findings position model assistance within a traceable realization and validation framework, linking generated recommendations to explicit system evidence and operational outcomes. The resulting workflow establishes a reproducible foundation for workload-aware kernel specialization under well-defined operational constraints.</jats:p>
title: IKC: Auditing LLM-Assisted Linux Kernel Configuration with Workload Evidence

items.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of large language models (LLMs) into urban mobility systems introduces new opportunities for simulating complex behavioral dynamics, particularly in ride-hailing markets. While these models show theoretical promise as autonomous proxies for human decision-makers, it is still unclear how effectively they navigate within strategic spatial economies. To determine if LLMs can authentically comprehend the values and replicate the routing behavior of human drivers under various economic context, this study evaluates four LLMs (ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini 3.0, DeepSeek V3.2, and Claude Sonnet 4.6). Using a stated-choice empirical framework, we subject these agents to combinations of fare schemes, surge multipliers, and varying passenger occupancies. By analyzing the fundamental trade-off between travel time and trip revenue, we compare the agents&apos; economic sensitivity against historical human taxi driver data. Our findings indicate that, at an aggregate level, LLM agents successfully interpret complex operating conditions and execute time-cost trade-offs comparable to human baselines. However, behavioral fidelity is highly model-dependent; notably, the routing consistency of DeepSeek V3.2 and Gemini 3.0 degrades under intense market incentives and heightened spatial complexity. Overall, our findings suggest that while LLMs demonstrate significant potential as behavioral simulators for transportation policy and planning, the their sensitivity to various economic contexts and cross-model heterogeneity necessitate more than simple performance alignment before deployment. Instead, their application in transportation networks should be supported by rigorous model-specific validation, staged and context-sensitive implementation, and adaptive governance mechanisms designed to ensure behavioral reliability, regulatory compatibility, and resilience to unintended strategic responses under dynamic market conditions.</jats:p>
title: Economic Incentives and Routing Behavior of LLM-Based Driver Agents in Ride-Hailing Markets

items.abstract: <jats:p>Traffic accident prevention requires not only accurate risk prediction but also the ability to communicate context-specific warnings to drivers in an understandable and timely manner. This study proposes a hybrid artificial intelligence framework that integrates machine learning–based accident severity modeling, real-time contextual data processing, and large language model (LLM)–driven semantic warning generation for intelligent driver assistance. The proposed framework combines historical accident records, spatial location data, driver-related variables, meteorological conditions, and real-time GPS information to identify high-risk road segments and generate personalized driver warnings.The study consists of three main stages. First, a survey of 576 drivers was conducted to examine risk perception, route familiarity, perceived adequacy of existing traffic safety measures, and acceptance of intelligent warning systems. The findings revealed strong driver demand for dynamic and context-aware warnings, particularly under heavy traffic conditions, unfamiliar routes, and accident-prone locations. Second, accident severity was modeled using machine learning algorithms, with the Random Forest model achieving the strongest classification performance, including a macro-averaged F1 score of 91.72%. Third, the predicted accident risk indicators were integrated with a multi-LLM semantic interpretation layer to transform numerical risk scores and contextual variables into concise, action-oriented, and personalized warning messages.The proposed mobile-based architecture delivers warnings through visual, auditory, and optional haptic interfaces when drivers approach high-risk locations. By combining predictive risk modeling with natural-language explanation and real-time contextual awareness, the framework moves beyond conventional static warning systems and offers a human-centered decision-support approach for intelligent transportation safety. The results suggest that LLM-augmented semantic fusion can improve the interpretability, personalization, and practical usability of traffic accident risk warning systems.</jats:p>
title: Multi-LLM Semantic Fusion for Context-Aware Traffic Accident Risk Prediction and Personalized Driver Warnings

items.abstract: <jats:p><p>This paper delves into the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) as they pertain to national security, with a particular emphasis on their integration into military applications. Through an in-depth analysis of the United States' progress in assimilating AI technologies into the battle space, the paper seeks to reinvigorate enthusiasm about the potential of AI in safeguarding national interests. Key aspects of this paper include the necessity of protecting AI systems from adversaries, as well as the inherent challenges and risks that come with integrating them into military operations. The paper concludes by underscoring the strategic significance of AI in the realm of national security and outlines a set of strategic imperatives for military leaders and policymakers to ensure success in this critical domain.</p></jats:p>
title: Optimizing National Security Strategies through LLM-Driven Artificial Intelligence Integration

items.abstract: <jats:p>Adversarial attacks pose an important threat to the security and trustworthiness of large language models (LLMs). These models are vulnerable to carefully engineered input designed to exploit their weaknesses, degrade system performance, and extract private information. Practical countermeasures need a strong offensive strategy that includes adversarial scenarios simulation to test how models hold up in various conditions. Adversarial data poisoning and evasion techniques are particularly useful as they can reveal strengths during training and inference processes, respectively. Through systematic identification and mitigation of every vulnerability, organizations can strengthen the model's robustness to real-world attacks. This technical framework also emphasizes the need to embed adversarial simulations into the security cycle of LLMs to prevent risks associated with malicious actors. Via iterative analysis, an organization can increase the robustness of a model and build a resilient infrastructure for secure implementation of LLMs in sensitive/high-level environments.</jats:p>

This study proposes an automated framework for systematically testing LLM-enabled mobile apps, focusing on identifying potential threats such as prompt injection, data leakage, unauthorized access, and adversarial manipulation. items.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Security attacks on large multi-tenant shared hosting sites, such as Linux based web servers, are rampant, severe and ongoing. These sites provide shared resources and are attacked constantly. Current reactive security products that usually notify of an attack hour after the fact are completely ineffective. This leaves hundreds of websites hosted on a server that have been compromised and not yet discovered. Methods: In this work, we perform an empirical study on five production Linux shared hosting servers hosting 707 websites over a 30-day time period (February 15 - March 17, 2026). We have collated and analysed authentication logs from all the five servers to measure attack volume, sources of attacks, and the types of credentials being attacked, as well as the current preventative measures deployed. A predictive security analytics framework is further proposed and validated against the measured attack landscape. Results: Failed SSH login attempts on all 5 servers for the period: 1,460,787 attempts originating from 1,674 IP addresses None of the servers had Fail2Ban engaged and there were no DROP rules on the firewalls. The most common username attempted was the root account along with a whole host of generic usernames (admin, user, ubuntu &amp; test) The attack intensity on each server over the period of time was quite varied with a high of 170,936 attempts in a single week on one server. Conclusions: We have demonstrated a significant and lasting vulnerability in shared hosting platforms using common configurations and lacking any preventative or proactive protection mechanisms. We showed a possible security approach for shared hosting based on log anomaly detection and associated remediation steps, and demonstrated steps towards more proactive and resilient security for shared hosting platforms.</jats:p>
title: Predictive Security Analytics for Large-Scale Multi-Tenant Linux Shared Hosting Environments: An Empirical Study

items.abstract: <jats:p>Wireless networks are an essential part of modern communication infrastructure, enabling ubiquitous connectivity for personal, professional, and industrial applications. From homes and offices to public spaces and IoT environments, wireless technologies have revolutionized the way data is transmitted and accessed. However, their inherent openness and reliance on shared mediums expose them to a multitude of security vulnerabilities. These vulnerabilities, if exploited, can lead to unauthorized access, sensitive data theft, and significant disruptions in operations, making wireless network security a critical concern.This chapter is dedicated to understanding and addressing these challenges by performing wireless penetration testing and security auditing using Linux-based tools. By leveraging tools such as scapy, aircrack-ng, and tcpdump within a Kali Linux environment, the project aims to uncover potential flaws in wireless networks, evaluate their implications, and propose actionable solutions. The study systematically investigates attack methods that are frequently exploited by attackers.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The article provides an overview of the key security aspects of the Linux operating system. The relevance of this work lies in the fact that in light of the rapid development of technology and increased threats in the field of information security, special attention is paid to mechanisms that ensure stable protection of data and system resources. The article begins by reviewing basic security principles such as the principle of least privilege and need-based access. Next, we look at modern authentication and authorization mechanisms, including the role of Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) and Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) multi-user rules. Particular attention is paid to access control systems, including mechanisms for managing access rights to files through the Discretionary Access Control (DAC) and Mandatory Access Control (MAC). The iptables and firewalld firewalls are analyzed as key tools for ensuring the security of network interactions. The article also covers current Linux security trends and challenges, as well as an overview of the latest kernel and software updates. Ultimately, the reader will gain a comprehensive understanding of Linux security mechanisms, allowing him to make informed decisions to effectively protect his systems and data.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Provenance-based host security has improved the detection, attribution, and reconstruction of suspicious activity, but translating heterogeneous runtime evidence into an explicit operational-risk decision remains less explored. This work presents CRRS, a causal–temporal runtimerisk framework for Linux hosts that integrates provenance context, behavioral novelty, causal evidence, temporal state, and operation sensitivity within a unified decision process. For each normalized event, CRRS updates an online provenance representation, estimates threat and temporal risk, and maps the resulting state to an operational response while preserving the supporting causal subgraph. The framework was evaluated across four heterogeneous Linux platforms using controlled benign and attack-related scenarios. Normal executions produced a mean maximum risk of 0.056940, suspicious executions reached 0.639267, and high-risk scenarios exceeded 0.90, yielding ALLOW, RESTRICT, and DENY, respectively. Across 100 holdout runs, CRRS produced 80 true positives and 20 true negatives with no classification errors under the controlled protocol, while cross-host risk variation remained below 2.3 × 10-4 . Mean userspace processing latency ranged from 13.37 to 90.83 𝜇s per event. Separate Ethernet validation further confirmed real inter-host network-event acquisition, with 30/30 successful TCP connections to each of two targets and mean throughputs of 350.77 and 86.27 Mbps. Overall, the results support CRRS as a stable and lightweight reasoning layer that extends provenance-based monitoring from detection and reconstruction toward actionable runtime risk assessment.</jats:p>
title: CRRS: A Causal–Temporal Runtime Risk Framework for Explainable Security Decisions on Linux Hosts

<jats:p>The prevailing literature suggests that large language model (LLM) systems remain vulnerable to prompt injection and other adversarial inputs, while existing LLM-based defenses do not provide deterministic assurance against such attacks. This paper therefore treats the LLM as insecure.It follows that a mechanism intended to secure an LLM must itself be independent of LLM technology. For sufficiently bounded domains, this paper proposes a deterministic front end that permits only validated, structured representations of user requests to cross a trust boundary protecting the LLM and security-critical information. The front end neither requires nor assumes an LLM; what consumes its output is irrelevant to its operation. 
<div>
 The paper further proposes that this front end can take the form of a deterministic natural-language interface (NLI), preserving the flexibility of an LLM-style prompt interface. Rather than attempting to anticipate all possible expressions, the NLI can be developed from a corpus of actual domain interactions using techniques derived from pre-LLM speech recognition and natural-language processing. The resulting classifier deterministically maps recognized input to permitted structured representations and rejects ambiguous, incomplete, or out-of-domain input.
</div>
<div>
 If sufficiently comprehensive, such an NLI may, at least for ordinary legitimate queries, be functionally indistinguishable to the user from a domainrestricted probabilistic LLM interface, while ensuring that unvalidated user input never crosses the trust boundary
</div></jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Abstract. The article discusses the main components of information security: confidentiality, integrity and accessibility. Passwords, encryption, authentication, and intrusion protection are methods designed to ensure confidentiality. Integrity means maintaining the data in its original state and preventing its modification: accidental or malicious. Ensuring the availability of information is understood as the compliance of network and computing resources with the expected amount of data access and the implementation of a backup policy for disaster recovery purposes. To ensure the security of information networks based on RedOS, the iptables utility, used to configure the Linux kernel firewall, has proven itself in the best way. Despite the fact that at first glance the implementation of IP routing in Linux may look quite complicated, in practice the most common use cases (NAT and/or basic Internet firewall) are much easier to implement. Iptables is a custom utility that allows you to work with chains/rules. The article describes in detail the principles of iptables operation, provides a detailed description of the NAT, mangle, filter, raw tables and chains. The NAT table is used to translate network addresses, mangle is used to distort packets, filter makes it possible to filter packets, raw and its chains are used before any other tables in netfilter. The input chain is used to process incoming packets and connections, forward — for passing packets, output — for outgoing packets. It is shown that to ensure the safety of the functioning of computer classes and the entire network infrastructure as a whole, only two tables are sufficient: filter and nat. Other tables are designed for complex configurations involving multiple routers and routing solutions. The results of using iptables based on the experience of administration of information networks based on RedOS in the federal state budgetary educational institution of higher education PSUTI are presented.</jats:p>
title: Iptables for Security of Linux-based Information Networks

<jats:p><p>The rapid enterprise deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous agentic AI systems has outpaced the security practices required to operate them safely. Traditional penetration testing methodologies — built on deterministic system assumptions — fail to address the probabilistic, natural-language attack surface introduced by AI deployments. This paper presents a structured, five-phase practitioner framework for LLM and agentic AI security testing, grounded in documented real-world attack patterns and aligned to OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025), OWASP Agentic Top 10 (2026), and MITRE ATLAS v5.1.0. The framework addresses four critical attack classes — indirect prompt injection via RAG corpus poisoning, agentic goal hijacking through multi-turn social engineering, system prompt leakage, and MCP tool poisoning — providing exploitation methodology, detection engineering guidance, and MITRE ATLAS technique mappings for each. Defensive countermeasures are presented across prevention, detection, and response layers, including sample detection logic for integration into SIEM and CI/CD pipelines. The paper establishes that organizations deploying AI systems without AI-specific security testing face material risks of data exfiltration, unauthorized autonomous action, and regulatory violation — and that a structured methodology mapped to existing frameworks is sufficient to close the execution gap.</p>
<p></p></jats:p>
title: Breaking AI: A Practitioner's Framework for LLM and Agentic AI Security Testing
The Role of Red Teaming in LLM Security

items.abstract: <jats:p>Trace-level characterization is a promising approach for understanding how adversarial influence propagates through resource-operating LLM agents, but current agent-security benchmarks and vulnerability disclosures collapse this propagation into binary outcomes or endpoint categories that obscure where attacks actually stopped. Recent benchmark-audit work has questioned the evidentiary support behind agent-security scores, yet the trace-level propagation structure inside those scores remains uncharacterized. This paper first proposes the Agentic Influence Propagation Framework (AIPF), a trace-level propagation framework with an applicability criterion based on three adversarial objective categories, an exposure marker X, three propagation levels (L1 operational commitment, L2 action materialization, L3 resource realization), and orthogonal episode annotations, and applies it to 180 AgentDojo traces through a three-annotator study spanning senior, junior, and non-specialist expertise. The analysis shows that 4 of 98 benchmark-defended traces reach L3 and 26 of 81 benchmark-successful traces show only shallow propagation, distinctions that the binary outcome collapses. Three case-study groups-a controlled CTF trace, a redacted cloud-agent vulnerability, and four public CVEs-further illustrate the vocabulary's reach beyond benchmark settings. This study provides a structured language for describing where agentic attacks stop and why, and extracts useful distinctions that can inform benchmark design, defence engineering, and agent-specific vulnerability reporting.</jats:p>
title: Beyond Binary Success: Propagation Profiles for LLM Agent Security Traces
